title: Chapter 42 — The Whiteness of the Whale
paragraphs: What the white whale meant to Ahab has been hinted at. What he was to me, at times, remains unsaid.

Beyond the more obvious fears that Moby Dick could stir in any man's soul, there was another thought — or rather a vague, nameless horror about him — that sometimes overpowered everything else with its intensity. Yet it was so mystical, so nearly impossible to put into words, that I almost despair of making it comprehensible. It was the whiteness of the whale that appalled me above all things. But how can I hope to explain myself here? And yet, in some dim, fumbling way, explain myself I must, or all these chapters will have been for nothing.

In many natural objects, whiteness enhances beauty, as if adding some special virtue of its own — in marble, in japonicas, in pearls. Various nations have recognized a royal superiority in this color. The grand old kings of Pegu placed the title "Lord of the White Elephants" above all their other titles of dominion. The modern kings of Siam unfurled the same snow-white creature on their royal banner. The Hanoverian flag bore the figure of a snow-white horse. The great Austrian Empire, heir to imperial Rome, chose the same imperial color. This supremacy extends even to the human race itself, granting the white man an assumed mastery over every darker people. Beyond all this, whiteness has been made a symbol of gladness — among the Romans, a white stone marked a joyful day. In other human customs and symbols, this same color represents many touching, noble things: the innocence of brides, the gentleness of old age. Among the Red Men of America, the gift of a white wampum belt was the deepest pledge of honor. In many lands, whiteness represents the majesty of Justice in the judge's ermine, and adds to the daily grandeur of kings and queens drawn by milk-white horses. Even in the highest mysteries of the most solemn religions, it has been made the symbol of divine purity and power. The Persian fire worshippers held the white forked flame holiest on the altar. In Greek mythology, great Jove himself took the form of a snow-white bull. Among the noble Iroquois, the midwinter sacrifice of the sacred White Dog was by far the holiest festival of their faith — that spotless, loyal creature being held the purest messenger they could send to the Great Spirit with the yearly news of their devotion. Directly from the Latin word for white, all Christian priests derive the name of one part of their sacred clothing — the alb, or tunic worn beneath the cassock. Among the holy ceremonies of the Roman Catholic faith, white is specially used in celebrating the Passion of our Lord. In the Vision of St. John, white robes are given to the redeemed, and the twenty-four elders stand clothed in white before the great white throne, and the Holy One sitting there is white like wool. Yet for all these accumulated associations with whatever is sweet, honorable, and sublime, there lurks something elusive in the deepest idea of this color that strikes more panic into the soul than the redness that frightens us in blood.

It is this elusive quality that causes the thought of whiteness, when separated from kinder associations and paired with any object terrible in itself, to heighten that terror to its furthest limits. Consider the white bear of the poles and the white shark of the tropics. What but their smooth, flaky whiteness makes them the supreme horrors they are? That ghastly whiteness gives them an awful mildness, even more repulsive than outright ferocity, in their dumb, gloating stare. The fierce-fanged tiger in his striped coat cannot stagger courage the way the white-shrouded bear or shark can.

Regarding the polar bear, someone might argue that it is not the whiteness alone that heightens the intolerable hideousness of that beast. Analyzed carefully, one might say that heightened horror only arises because the creature's mindless ferocity is dressed in the fleece of heavenly innocence and love. By bringing together two such opposite emotions in our minds, the polar bear frightens us with so unnatural a contrast. But even granting all this — without the whiteness, you would not feel that intensified terror.

As for the white shark, the white gliding ghostliness of that creature at rest, when seen in its ordinary moods, strangely matches the same quality in the polar bear. The French capture this perfectly in the name they give that fish. The Roman Catholic mass for the dead begins with "Requiem eternam" — eternal rest — from which "Requiem" names the mass itself and any other funeral music. In reference to the white, silent stillness of death in this shark, and the mild deadliness of its habits, the French call it Requin.

Think of the albatross. Where do those clouds of spiritual wonder and pale dread come from, in which that white phantom sails through every imagination? It was not Coleridge who first cast that spell, but God's great, unsparing poet laureate: Nature.

I remember the first albatross I ever saw. It was during a long gale, in waters near the Antarctic seas. From my morning watch below, I climbed to the cloud-covered deck. There, thrown upon the main hatches, I saw a regal, feathery thing of spotless whiteness, with a hooked, noble bill. At intervals, it spread its vast archangel wings as if to embrace some holy ark. Wonderful flutterings and throbbings shook it. Though physically unharmed, it cried out like some king's ghost in supernatural anguish. Through its indescribable, strange eyes, I felt I glimpsed secrets known only to God. Like Abraham before the angels, I bowed. The white thing was so white, its wings so wide, and in those forever-exiled waters, I had lost all the warped memories of customs and civilization. I gazed long at that miracle of feathers. I cannot describe — only hint at — the things that shot through me then. But at last I stirred and asked a sailor what bird this was. A goney, he said. Goney! I had never heard the name. Could this glorious creature be utterly unknown to people ashore? Never! But later I learned that "goney" was a seaman's name for albatross. So Coleridge's wild Rhyme could have had nothing to do with the mystical impressions I felt when I saw that bird on our deck. I had not then read the poem, nor knew the bird to be an albatross. Yet in saying this, I only shine a brighter light on the noble merit of both poem and poet.

I maintain, then, that in the bird's wondrous bodily whiteness chiefly lurks the secret of its spell. This is further proven by the fact that there are birds called grey albatrosses. I have seen them often, but never with the emotions I felt when I beheld the Antarctic fowl.

But how had the mystical creature been caught? Whisper it not, and I will tell you: with a treacherous hook and line, as the bird floated on the sea. Eventually the Captain made a postman of it, tying a lettered leather tag around its neck with the ship's time and position, then letting it go free. But I have no doubt that leather tag, meant for human hands, was removed in Heaven when the white bird flew up to join the wing-folding, worshipping cherubim.

Most famous in Western history and Native American traditions is the White Steed of the Prairies — a magnificent milk-white horse, large-eyed, small-headed, broad-chested, with the dignity of a thousand monarchs in his proud, scornful bearing. He was the chosen king of vast herds of wild horses whose pastures were bounded only by the Rocky Mountains and the Alleghenies. At their blazing head he led them westward like that chosen star which every evening guides the hosts of light. The flashing waterfall of his mane, the curving comet of his tail, dressed him in finery more splendid than anything gold and silver workers could have furnished. He was a supreme, archangelic vision of that unfallen western world, which to the eyes of old trappers and hunters revived the glories of those first days when Adam walked as majestic as a god, bold-browed and fearless as this mighty horse. Whether marching with his lieutenants and generals at the head of endless columns streaming across the plains like a river, or whether with his surrounding subjects grazing all around at the horizon, reviewing them at a gallop with warm nostrils reddening through his cool milky whiteness — in whatever form he appeared, he was always an object of trembling reverence and awe to the bravest Indians. And it cannot be questioned, from what legendary records tell of this noble horse, that it was his spiritual whiteness above all that clothed him with divinity. And that divinity contained something which, though commanding worship, at the same time enforced a certain nameless terror.
But there are other cases where whiteness loses all that added strange glory it possesses in the White Steed and the Albatross.

What is it about the albino man that so particularly repels and often shocks the eye, so that he is sometimes despised by his own family? It is the whiteness that covers him, the very thing expressed by his name. The albino is as well-built as other men — he has no real deformity — and yet this all-pervading whiteness makes him more strangely hideous than the ugliest birth defect. Why should this be?

In quite different ways, Nature in her subtlest but no less vicious workings does not fail to enlist this supreme attribute of the terrible among her forces. From its snowy appearance, the armored ghost of the Southern Seas has been called the White Squall. And in some historical cases, human cruelty has not overlooked so powerful a tool. How wildly it heightens the effect of that passage in Froissart, when, masked in the snowy emblem of their faction, the desperate White Hoods of Ghent murder their magistrate in the marketplace.

In certain things, the common inherited experience of all humanity bears witness to the supernatural quality of this color. It can hardly be doubted that the one visible quality in the appearance of the dead that most horrifies the viewer is the marble paleness lingering there — as if that pallor were as much the mark of terror in the next world as it is of mortal fear in this one. From the pallor of the dead, we borrow the color of the shroud we wrap them in. Even in our superstitions we throw the same snowy cloak around our ghosts — all phantoms rise in a milk-white fog. And while these terrors grip us, let us add that even the king of terrors himself, as portrayed by the evangelist, rides on a pale horse.

Therefore, whatever grand or gracious thing a person may symbolize through whiteness in other moods, no one can deny that in its deepest, most idealized meaning, it summons a peculiar specter to the soul.

But though this point is settled beyond dispute, how can any mortal account for it? To analyze it seems impossible. Can we, then, by citing some of those cases where this thing of whiteness — though for the time mostly or entirely stripped of all associations meant to make it fearful, yet still found to work the same spell on us, however softened — can we hope to stumble upon some clue that leads us to the hidden cause we seek?

Let us try. But in a matter like this, subtlety speaks to subtlety, and without imagination, no one can follow another into these halls. And though many of the imaginative impressions about to be presented may have been shared by most people, few were probably fully aware of them at the time, and therefore may not be able to recall them now.

Why does the man of untrained imagination, who happens to know little about the particular character of the holiday, find that the mere mention of Whitsuntide conjures in his mind such long, dreary, speechless processions of slow-walking pilgrims, downcast and hooded in fresh-fallen snow? Or why does the unread, unsophisticated Protestant of the American heartland find that the passing mention of a White Friar or a White Nun summons such an eyeless statue in his soul?

Or what is it — beyond the traditions of imprisoned warriors and kings, which do not fully explain it — that makes the White Tower of London strike the imagination of an untraveled American so much more powerfully than its neighboring landmarks, the Byward Tower, or even the Bloody Tower? And those sublimer towers, the White Mountains of New Hampshire — why does their bare mention send, in certain moods, such a gigantic ghostliness over the soul, while the thought of Virginia's Blue Ridge is full of a soft, dewy, distant dreaminess? Or why, regardless of all geography, does the name of the White Sea cast such a spectral pall over the imagination, while the Yellow Sea lulls us with mortal thoughts of long, mild afternoons on the waves, followed by the most brilliant yet sleepiest of sunsets? Or, to choose a purely fanciful example, why does "the tall pale man" of the Harz forests in old Central European fairy tales, whose unchanging pallor glides silently through the green of the groves — why is this phantom more terrible than all the whooping demons of the Blocksberg?

It is not entirely the memory of her cathedral-toppling earthquakes, nor the stampedes of her frantic seas, nor the dryness of skies that never weep rain, nor the sight of her wide fields of leaning spires, wrenched capstones, and drooping crosses — like the tilted yards of anchored fleets — and her suburban avenues of house-walls fallen against each other like a tossed deck of cards. These things alone do not make tearless Lima the strangest, saddest city you can see. For Lima has taken the white veil. And there is a higher horror in the whiteness of her grief. Old as Pizarro, this whiteness keeps her ruins forever new. It admits no cheerful green of natural decay. It spreads over her broken walls the rigid pallor of a stroke that freezes its own distortions.

I know that to ordinary perception, whiteness is not admitted to be the prime agent in heightening the terror of things already terrible. Nor does the unimaginative mind find any terror in those sights whose awfulness, to another mind, consists almost entirely in this one quality — especially when displayed in any form approaching silence or universality. What I mean by these two statements may perhaps be clarified by the following examples.

First: The sailor, when approaching foreign coasts, if he hears the roar of breakers at night, snaps to alertness and feels just enough fear to sharpen all his senses. But under exactly the same conditions, let him be called from his hammock to see his ship sailing through a midnight sea of milky whiteness — as if herds of combed white bears were swimming around him from encircling headlands — and he feels a silent, superstitious dread. The shrouded phantom of the whitened waters is as horrible to him as a real ghost. In vain the sounding lead assures him he is still in deep water. Heart and helm both fail him. He never rests until blue water is beneath him again. Yet where is the sailor who will tell you, "Sir, it was not so much the fear of hitting hidden rocks as the fear of that hideous whiteness that shook me"?

Second: To the native peoples of Peru, the constant sight of the snow-crowned Andes holds no dread, except perhaps in imagining the eternal frozen desolation that reigns at such heights, and the natural thought of how terrifying it would be to lose oneself in such inhuman solitudes. Much the same goes for the frontiersman of the West, who views with relative indifference an endless prairie sheeted in driven snow, with no shadow of tree or branch to break the fixed trance of whiteness. Not so the sailor, beholding the Antarctic seas. There, by some infernal trick of frost and air, he — shivering and half-shipwrecked — instead of seeing rainbows that speak of hope and comfort in his misery, beholds what looks like a boundless graveyard grinning at him with its lean ice monuments and splintered crosses.
But you say, I think, that this bleached chapter about whiteness is just a white flag flown by a coward's soul. You surrender to despair, Ishmael.

Tell me, then — why does a strong young colt, born in some peaceful Vermont valley, far from all predators — why is it that on the sunniest day, if you shake a fresh buffalo hide behind him so he cannot even see it but only smells its wild animal musk — why will he bolt, snort, and paw the ground in frenzy with bulging eyes? He has no memory of being attacked by wild creatures in his green northern home. The strange muskiness cannot remind him of any past danger. What does this New England colt know of the black bison herds of distant Oregon?

Nothing. But here you see, even in a speechless animal, the instinct of knowing the demonic forces in the world. Though thousands of miles from Oregon, when he smells that savage musk, the charging, goring bison herds are as real to him as they are to the abandoned wild foal on the prairies, which at this very moment they may be trampling into dust.

So it is: the muffled rolling of a milky sea, the bleak rustling of frosted mountain peaks, the desolate shifting of windblown prairie snows — all these are to Ishmael what the shaking of that buffalo robe is to the frightened colt.

Though neither of us knows where the nameless things lie, of which these mystic signs give such hints — yet with me, as with the colt, somewhere those things must exist. In many of its aspects, this visible world seems formed in love. The invisible spheres were formed in fright.

But we have not yet solved the spell of this whiteness or learned why it appeals with such power to the soul. And stranger still, far more ominous — why, as we have seen, it is at once the most meaningful symbol of spiritual things, the very veil of the Christian's God, and yet at the same time the intensifying agent in things most appalling to humanity.

Is it that by its vagueness it hints at the heartless voids and immensities of the universe, and so stabs us from behind with the thought of annihilation when we gaze into the white depths of the Milky Way? Or is it that whiteness, in its essence, is not so much a color as the visible absence of color — and at the same time the sum of all colors? Is that why there is such a meaningful blankness in a wide landscape of snow — a colorless all-color of atheism from which we recoil? And when we consider the theory of the natural philosophers, that all other earthly colors — every stately or lovely display, the sweet tints of sunset skies and woods, the gilded velvets of butterflies, the rosy cheeks of young girls — are all merely surface illusions, not actually part of the substances themselves, but only painted on from outside? So that all of glorified Nature paints herself like a prostitute, whose attractions conceal nothing but the charnel-house within? And when we go further and consider that the mystical cosmetic that produces every one of her colors — the great principle of light — forever remains white or colorless in itself, and if it touched all objects without any medium, would paint even tulips and roses with its own blank shade? Considering all this, the paralyzed universe lies before us like a leper. And like stubborn travelers in Lapland who refuse to wear tinted protective glasses, the wretched unbeliever stares himself blind at the monumental white shroud that wraps the entire view around him. And of all these things, the albino whale was the symbol. Do you wonder, then, at the fiery hunt?
